title: In the bleak midwinter (Rossetti, 1872)
hook: what can I give him, poor as I am? give my heart
tomorrow: can a worn-out world still be charged with something?

segments.voice: Yesterday the pilgrim's prayer settled into the beat of his heart: the prayer prays itself. Today, a different question about a heart: what to do with it when your hands are empty.

A friend's birthday, and the group chat is splitting the cost of a gift, and your share is more than your account holds. Or someone you love is going through something no store sells a fix for. Empty hands are an old problem. Christina Rossetti, an English poet, wrote a Christmas poem that walks straight into it, starting in the coldest weather she could find: earth hard as iron, water like a stone, “Snow had fallen, snow on snow.”
screen: `YOUR SHARE IS MORE THAN YOU HAVE.` → `NOTHING TO BUY THAT FIXES IT.` → `SNOW ON SNOW.`

segments.voice: Into that cold she sets a newborn. Heaven can't hold him, the poem says, nor earth sustain him, and yet a stable was enough. A small place for a great guest. Then the last verse asks the question: “What can I give Him, Poor as I am?” Rossetti looks around the stable for answers. “If I were a shepherd I would bring a lamb; If I were a Wise Man I would do my part.” She's thinking of the people in the Gospel stories who came with something. Luke's shepherds “came with haste.” Matthew's wise men opened their treasures: “gold, and frankincense, and myrrh.” But she is neither. No lamb, no gold. And then the turn, as plain as a child's answer: “Yet what I can I give Him: Give my heart.” Notice what she doesn't say. She doesn't call the lamb and the gold useless, or say the shepherds had it wrong. Those are real gifts. She just finds that the poorest person in the poem still has one thing to bring. Not a grand feeling, either. A heart, given as it is, on a cold night, to someone who came into a small place. Nobody arrives at that stable with enough. They arrive with what they have.
screen: `A SMALL PLACE FOR A GREAT GUEST.` · `WHAT CAN I GIVE HIM?` · `NO LAMB, NO GOLD.` · `A HEART, GIVEN AS IT IS.` · then, large: `GIVE MY HEART.`

segments.voice: If there's paper near you, write Rossetti's question at the top: what can I give? Under it, write one thing you could give today that costs nothing, an hour, a call, your full attention, and the name of who it's for. Then rest your hands open on the page for the rest of the sit.
In the bleak midwinter. Rossetti's cold-weather Christmas poem, ending on the one gift the poorest still has.
For the road: give my heart. The poorest person in the poem still has that to bring. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: a classmate's family is going through a hard month, and everyone is chipping in money. you can't. what fits Rossetti's last verse?
options: stay out of it; with no money, there's nothing you can really bring.
give what you do have: show up, help out, write them a note.

fork.reveal: Rossetti doesn't say the lamb and the gold don't matter. she finds the one thing the poorest still has, and brings it: give my heart.

chat.says: doctor says Pop can't sit through the concert. i wanted to give him something special and i've got nothing.
options: You've got the song. Sing it for him on the porch. That's giving what you have.
Buy him something nice instead, so he knows the concert still counts.
Let it go. If he can't come, there's no gift that fits anymore.
chat.meaning: Rossetti has no lamb and no gold, so she gives what she has: her heart. A gift doesn't need money to be real.
